units.open: In this paper we present a computerized model for studying serial crime patterns.
units.close: Our models give law enforcement agencies an estimate as to where they could patrol with the highest likelihood of apprehending the criminal, as well as where they should conduct their investigation into the residence of the criminal.

units.open: The beginning of our paper will be devoted to presenting the theoretical frame- work and an outline of our computer implementation.
units.close: The later sections of our paper will be devoted to applying our model to famous notable criminal cases and assessing the accuracy of the model.

heading: 2 Mapping Crime and the Road Metric (2.1 Road Metric)
evidence: 2 Mapping Crime and the Road Metric We used the mathematical software Sage to create a map of the area surrounding serial criminal incidents.
For each map M, we computed a road metric d : M × M →R+.
• Time spent on side streets is proportional to the Manhattan metric since side streets are often organized into a grid shape, • Time spent on the freeway is proportional to the Euclidean dis- tance.
Given points a and b on the map, we compute the road metric as follows: …
1. For each vertex v in our highway system (which correspond to entrances or exits on the freeway), we compute the Manhattan distances M(v, a) and M(v, b).

2. For each pair of vertices v1, v2, we apply Dijkstra’s algorithm to ﬁnd the shortest path (taking into consideration the lengths of the edge segments) on the graph of our highway system from v1 to v2.

3. Then our road metric is deﬁned as   v1,v2{M(a, v1) + E(v1, v2) + M(v2, b)}, M(a, b) d(a, b) = min min , or in other words, the minimum of the fastest way to take the highway, and taking a route which avoids the highway.

heading: 6 Improving the Model (6.1 Expanding the Road Metric, 6.2 Profiling Potential Victims, 6.3 Improving Computational Efficiency, 6.4 Testing to Choose Optimal Parameters)
evidence: Figure 12: Rossmo’s probability estimate as a surface.
One of the most novel aspects of our approach was the design of the road metric to accurately estimate the cost of travel to a criminal.
As we observed in the case of the Atlanta Child Murderer, the kernel method was unable to predict a relatively unexpected kill site (in terms of pure ge- ography).
Our algorithm saves time by overlaying a grid on the map of the region and saving the distance between every pair of cells.

With a more eﬃcient algorithm (or implementation that is faster than what Sage has available) for measuring distances in the road metric, we can make our grids ﬁner and improve the precision of our model.

6.4 Testing to Choose Optimal Parameters Since we had a limited amount of time to perform computationally hard tests, our empirically-determined choice for the variance function h in the kernel method may be far from optimal.

heading: 11 Executive Summary
evidence: Overview: Strengths and Weaknesses of the Model …
This paper presents a model of where a violent serial criminal will strike next, based upon the locations and times of his previous crimes.
• The model contains no arbitrary parameters.
• The model can estimate the level of conﬁdence in its predictions.
• The model understands that police have limited resources.
At the same time, it must be observed that our model contains some fundamental limita- tions: …
• The model is only clearly applicable to violent serial criminals.
The model cannot predict when a criminal will strike.
• The model cannot make use of underlying map data.
The model has not been validated on a large set of empirical data.

In addition, the standard warnings that would apply to any geographic proﬁling scheme apply: The output should not be treated as a single prediction, but rather as a tool to help prioritize areas of focus.
Inputs Our model requires the coordinate locations of a serial criminal’s previous offenses, as well as the order in which these crimes were committed.
1. The Criminal will tend to strike at locations around one or more “anchor points.” (often, the criminal’s house).
2. Around this anchor point, there may be a “buffer zone” within which he will not strike.
3. If the criminal has multiple anchor points, the regions around those from which he has struck most often or most recently are more likely.
Method The algorithm implements two different models, and then decides which is better.
• In the ﬁrst method, we assume the criminal has a single anchor point, and build likelihood regions around the anchor point based on the distribution of his past crimes.
• In the second, we assume multiple anchor points, calculate the best number of anchor points to use, and determine likelihood around each point individually.
Finally, the algorithm tests both models to see how well they would have predicted the previous crimes, and uses the model with the better track record.

heading: Summary (p1) and Executive Summary (pp2-3)
evidence: Summary We develop geographical proﬁling methods that determine the probable lo- cation of a serial criminal’s next crime based on the spatiotemporal data of their previous crimes.
We consider standard deviation, centralization, and probability distance methods for prioritizing a given search area.
The performance of a geographical proﬁling method is based on its ef- fectiveness in narrowing down a particular search area into regions likely to contain the next crime location.
Executive Summary We have developed models to be used in an open investigation of a serial criminal.
Our models use the locations and times of previous crimes committed by a serial criminal in order to predict the likely next target location.
• Centralization models: These models are based on the assumption that a serial criminal’s activity is centered around a point.
• Probability distance models: In these models, the closer a location is to previous crimes, the higher the probability the serial criminal will strike there next.
• Time-based models: In these models, a location’s proximity to recent crimes is weighted more heavily than its proximity to crimes in the distant past.
• Aggregate models: These models combine the above models.
There are multiple factors to consider when deciding if a particular model is applicable to a serial criminal investigation: …
• Evidence of serial nature: Our models assume that all of the ob- served crimes were committed by one criminal.
• Accuracy score: Our models provide a statistic that estimates their accuracy as applied to the serial criminal under investigation.
• Available resources: Our models prioritize the search area such that the next crime location is on average in the top 10% of the prioritized search area.
If it is determined that our models are applicable to a serial criminal inves- tigation, then there are multiple limitations of our models which need to be taken into consideration: …
• Our models do not take into account relevant geographical information: For example, if you know the serial criminal is targeting banks, our models do not take this into account.

• Our models do not take into account relevant information about the criminal: The average distance that a serial criminal trav- els to commit a crime depends on the type of crime and characteristics of the criminal, including gender, race, and age.

• Our computer models may not outperform geographical pro- ﬁling techniques employed by a human: Research has suggested that complex computer geographical proﬁling methods are no more accurate than an investigator with minimal training in geographical proﬁling …
Overall, we recommend that our geographical proﬁling models not be used as the only tool used in a serial criminal investigation.

units.open: There are multiple factors to consider when deciding if a particular model is applicable to a serial criminal investigation: …
units.close: There are multiple factors to consider when deciding if a particular model is applicable to a serial criminal investigation:

units.open: • Evidence of serial nature: Our models assume that all of the ob- served crimes were committed by one criminal.
units.close: If there is a strong reason to doubt this assumption, such as the presence of a copy-cat criminal, then our models are not applicable.

units.open: • Accuracy score: Our models provide a statistic that estimates their accuracy as applied to the serial criminal under investigation.
units.close: If our models would not have performed well in predicting the locations of this serial criminal’s past crimes, there is no reason to believe that our models would accurately predict the location of the criminal’s next crime.

units.open: • Available resources: Our models prioritize the search area such that the next crime location is on average in the top 10% of the prioritized search area.
units.close: If this search area is still too large to cover, then our models are still applicable but may not yield optimal results.

units.open: If it is determined that our models are applicable to a serial criminal inves- tigation, then there are multiple limitations of our models which need to be taken into consideration: …
units.close: If it is determined that our models are applicable to a serial criminal inves- tigation, then there are multiple limitations of our models which need to be taken into consideration:

units.open: • Our models do not take into account relevant geographical information: For example, if you know the serial criminal is targeting banks, our models do not take this into account.
units.close: In this example, a list of bank locations can be cross-referenced against the prioritized search area given by our models to determine the banks that are likely to be targeted next.

units.open: • Our models do not take into account relevant information about the criminal: The average distance that a serial criminal trav- els to commit a crime depends on the type of crime and characteristics of the criminal, including gender, race, and age.
units.close: Our models assume no information of this type is known about the criminal.

units.open: • Our computer models may not outperform geographical pro- ﬁling techniques employed by a human: Research has suggested that complex computer geographical proﬁling methods are no more accurate than an investigator with minimal training in geographical proﬁling …
units.close: … er models may not outperform geographical pro- ﬁling techniques employed by a human: Research has suggested that complex computer geographical proﬁling methods are no more accurate than an investigator with minimal training in geographical proﬁling techniques.

units.open: Overall, we recommend that our geographical proﬁling models not be used as the only tool used in a serial criminal investigation.
units.close: It is our hope that our models can further aid law enforcement agencies in their pursuit of serial criminals.

heading: 1 Introduction
evidence: Serial criminals present a unique challenge to law enforcement agencies.
In order to better utilize limited law enforcement resources in a serial criminal investigation, geographical proﬁling can be used to determine likely next crime locations.
In this paper we examine diﬀerent geographical proﬁling methodologies and compare their ability to predict the location of a serial criminal’s next crime.

heading: 2 Problem Background (2.1 Terminology, 2.2 Survey of Current Literature)
evidence: • Serial Criminal: A serial criminal is a habitual oﬀender who commits three or more related crimes over a span of time [1, 4].
• Spatiotemporal Data: The locations and corresponding times of crimes committed by a serial criminal.
• Spatial Behavior: The spatial behavior of a serial criminal describes how the serial criminal chooses crime locations [5, 6].
• Geographical Proﬁling Method: A geographical proﬁling method is a particular methodology for modeling the spatial behavior of a serial criminal.

There is an ongoing debate as to the eﬀectiveness of diﬀerent geographical proﬁling methodologies.

units.open: Unfortunately, the data can be misleading.
units.close: This is unavoidable: there is no method (as far as we can tell) to accurately guess the killer’s “hub” location if it is suﬃciently removed from the locations of the crimes themselves.

units.close: Another possible explanation is that the increased number of calculations required to generate the estimated next location resulted in signiﬁcantly smaller random ﬂuctuations, meaning that the data is “smoother” and therefore more likely to behave well.

heading: 6.2 Additional Layers (redundancy, special case, runtime)
evidence: Although the algorithm described in Section 6.1 can successfully cover any given percentage of users, it often employs a number of repeaters which cover only a relatively small fraction of the population.

The reasoning is as follows: if an average repeater is malfunctioning with some fraction p of the time, the expected loss of utility (ignoring regions of overlap) is pn, where n is the number of people covered by the repeater’s signal.
To clarify the workings of our algorithm, we present pseudocode describing its pre- optimization behavior in Program 2.
Basic Coverage as a Special Case In addition to maximizing the total utility of the covering, the above pseudocode can actually be used to satisfy the two goals mentioned in Section 6.1.
As the overall structure of the main loop’s body has not changed signiﬁcantly since previous runtime analysis, the runtime of each iteration is again O(r2s4).
In order to successfully deal with this approximately-quartic runtime, various optimiza- tions had to be made.

heading: 8 Conclusion and Discussion
evidence: In this paper, we propose a two-tiered network model, where lower-power users can communicate with one another through repeaters.
Compared with the related model for sensor wireless networks and mobile communication networks, our model is more general.
There are also two considerable weaknesses in this work.

units.open: In this paper, we propose a two-tiered network model, where lower-power users can communicate with one another through repeaters.
units.close: For example, in the case of 10000 users, given a user, the probability this user can successfully send signal to a random position in the considered area is about 97.12%.

units.open: Compared with the related model for sensor wireless networks and mobile communication networks, our model is more general.
units.close: Another advantage of the algorithm is that it can be widely applied since it does not require any specific geographical features of the considered area, while many efficient circle-covering algorithms only work well for squares.

units.open: There are also two considerable weaknesses in this work.
units.close: Secondly, our model is largely simplified, which have not taken into account the heterogeneity of users and repeaters, or the wave reflection and refraction by atmosphere.

note: Three concluding units: the model and both methods restated with the 97.12 percent reachability figure for 10000 users (225), the comparison with sensor-network and mobile-communication models plus the speed advantage over simulated annealing and the local-optimum advantage over the earlier refinement algorithm (226), and the two admitted weaknesses, no effective algorithm for global reachability without adding repeaters, and a model that ignores user and repeater heterogeneity, wave reflection and atmospheric refraction (227). heading: 1.3 Constraints and 1.4 Assumptions
evidence: The problem specifies the following constraints: • Trips begin at First Launch and end at Final Exit – exactly 225 miles downstream.
• We have the ability to determine the proportion of oar-powered river rafts to motorized boats that go onto the river each day.
• The duration of trips is constrained to the following values: 12 or 18 days for groups travelling by oar-powered river rafts, and 6 or 12 days for those travelling by motorized boat.
• There can only be one group per campsite per night.
• Each day, groups may only move downstream or remain in their current campsite -- they may not move back up stream.
• Groups heading downstream can only travel the river between 8am and 6pm.
• Groups will never travel further than the amount of miles that they can feasibly travel in a single day.
• Variables which could influence maximum daily travel distance, such as weather and river conditions, are ignored.
• Campsites are distributed uniformly so that the distance between campsites is 225/𝑌 (the length of the river divided by the number of camp sites between the start and end of the river).
• A group must reach the end of the river on the final day of its trip: o A group will not leave the river early even if they are able to.

units.open: The problem specifies the following constraints: • Trips begin at First Launch and end at Final Exit – exactly 225 miles downstream.
units.close: • No two sets of campers can occupy the same site at the same time.

units.open: • We have the ability to determine the proportion of oar-powered river rafts to motorized boats that go onto the river each day.
units.close: Moving a high volume of groups down the river in a satisfactory time becomes an issue if too many oar-powered boats are launched with short trip lengths.

units.open: • The duration of trips is constrained to the following values: 12 or 18 days for groups travelling by oar-powered river rafts, and 6 or 12 days for those travelling by motorized boat.
units.close: This is a simplification which allows our model to produce more meaningful results while preserving the ability to compare the effect of varying inputs.

units.open: • There can only be one group per campsite per night.
units.close: Our algorithm only considers campsites which are empty as open campsites that groups can move to, which is consistent with the desires of the river manager.

units.open: • Each day, groups may only move downstream or remain in their current campsite -- they may not move back up stream.
units.close: This allows us to restrict the flow of groups on the river to a single direction which greatly simplifies the ways in which we can move groups from campsite to campsite.

units.open: • Groups heading downstream can only travel the river between 8am and 6pm.
units.close: This allows us to determine the set of groups that can reasonably reach a given campsite.

units.open: • Groups will never travel further than the amount of miles that they can feasibly travel in a single day.
units.close: As the previous assumption states, this is 36 miles per day for oar-powered river rafts and 72 miles per day for motorized boats in our model.

units.open: • Variables which could influence maximum daily travel distance, such as weather and river conditions, are ignored.
units.close: There is no way of accurately including this in the model with the amount of given information about the Big Long River.

units.open: • Campsites are distributed uniformly so that the distance between campsites is 225/𝑌 (the length of the river divided by the number of camp sites between the start and end of the river).
units.close: This assumption allows us to easily represent the river as an array of campsites that are equally spaced out in our computer simulation.

units.open: • A group must reach the end of the river on the final day of its trip: o A group will not leave the river early even if they are able to.
units.close: o A group will not have a finish date that is past their desired trip length.

note: The eight constraints restated as a bullet list (44-52), then nine assumptions, each a bullet with its justification: known propulsion proportions (53-56), the duration menu of 12 or 18 nights oar-powered and 6 or 12 motorized (57-60), one group per campsite per night (61-63), downstream-only movement (64-67), the 8am to 6pm travelling window giving 36 and 72 mile days (68-72), no group exceeding that daily distance (73-75), weather and river conditions ignored (76-78), campsite spacing of 225 over Y (79-82), and every group finishing on its final day (83-86). heading: 4.1 The Grand Canyon
evidence: The Grand Canyon is an ideal case study for our model.
Using the parameters of the Grand Canyon, we tested our model by running a number of simulations.
During its summer season, the Grand Canyon typically places six new groups on the water each day [3], so we use this value for our first simulation.

Our model predicts the number of groups that make it off the end of the river (completed trips), how many of those trips arrive past their desired end date (late trips), and the number of groups which did not make it off the waitlist (total left on waitlist).
Figure 4.1: We predict that a maximum of 18 groups can be sent down the river each day.
We conclude that the maximum carrying capacity of the Grand Canyon is around 3000, and is achieved by sending 18 new groups down the river each day.
Notice that some groups are still on the river when our simulation ends.

heading: 6 Limitations and Error Analysis (6.1 overestimation, 6.2 environment, 6.3 river speed)
evidence: Our model has several limitations. It assumes that the capacity of the river is constrained only by number of campsites, trip durations, and transportation methods.
Our case study of the Grand Canyon is evidence that our model omits variables.
Another variable our model ignores is the speed of the river.

units.open: Our model has several limitations. It assumes that the capacity of the river is constrained only by number of campsites, trip durations, and transportation methods.
units.close: Because of this, our model may overestimate the maximum number of trips possible over long periods of time.

units.open: Our case study of the Grand Canyon is evidence that our model omits variables.
units.close: Our results represent a maximum number of trips, based on available campsites, and should be considered along with other factors.

units.open: Another variable our model ignores is the speed of the river.
units.close: Again, the results of our model don’t reflect these issues.

units.open: This was extened to a priority model, which gives priority to the trips that have to go the farthest each day.
units.close: If two trips try to stop at the same campsite, then this algorithm arranges them so that they do not cross over and therefore less trips are discarded.

units.open: The next model that was attempted was a density perturbation algorithm.
units.close: If trips try to move to locations that are too close to each other, then a density vector is created that ﬁnds how close the trips are to each other and moves them apart so that a one-to-one mapping to the campsites can be found.

units.open: The last model that was created was a bone growth model.
units.close: This model is a greedy deterministic model that is very sensitive to the initial bone structure, but guarentees a local op- timal solution.

• The model should maximize the carrying eﬃciency of the white water river rafting system while maintaining high levels of customer satisfac- tion.
• The model should satisfy customer demands in terms of oﬀered trips.
• The model should perform eﬀectively under a wide range of variable operating conditions.
The model should also present a contingency plan for conditions that impede the ﬂow of visitors down the river, such as weather.
• The model must be easy to implement.
Scheduling: Static vs Dynamic Approaches We have up until now not considered the concept of “scheduling” visitors to the white water river park.

To proceed, we must evaluate two diﬀerent strategies to schedule visitors to camp sites - the static approach and the dynamic approach.
Static approaches are the most widespread of scheduling strategies, and are extensively used by white water rafting companies across the nation.
Visitors can pay to participate in one of these speciﬁc trips.
• Static approaches reduce the number of visitors who can participate in rafting activities during the rafting season.
Unlike the static system, the dynamic system emphasizes maximizing the num- ber of trip options oﬀered to visitors.

heading: 7 The Model: A Cellular Automaton-like Strategy (7.1 to 7.4)
evidence: 7 The Model: A Cellular Automaton-like Strategy We here describe our dynamic model of white water river rafting scheduling over the course of a rafting season.

Our model possesses certain similarities to a one-dimensional cellular automaton, as well as some diﬀerent characteristics that make it uniquely suited to our problem: • We describe the river as a one-dimensional array containing Y cells.
• We will deﬁne a visitor object that can occupy cells in the river array.
• There are a discrete number of visitor objects that can be constructed.
• Every iteration will be considered one day in real time.
• From day to day, we will apply a series of rules designed to move each visitor object in the river array to an unoccupied space in the array that is downstream from the visitor’s current position.
• Every day, new visitors will also be added to the array based on the governing rules of the automaton-like structure.
• To account for the discrete nature of the array, continuous distances are expressed as a function of the number of camp sites Y .

The cellular automaton-like model is highly ﬂexible in its ability to test a variety of conditions.

• The number of days traveled, Di, and the number of days left to complete the trip, Dr.

heading: Summary (MCM summary sheet)
evidence: Aimed to look for the “best all time college coach” for the previous century, we employ methods in grey and fuzzy fields to build an evaluation model and give out coach ranks in various sports fields by massive calculating.
In order to simplify our model, we firstly adopt AHP to filter factors and determine seven most influential criterion, including coaching time, gender, etc.
Based on AHP Model, two advanced models are proposed to rank college coaches.
Considering time line horizon’s impact on evaluating results, we augment our model by revising the weights and re-rank, based on membership function.
Our paper considers multiple factors, employs several models and does plenty of calculations, which makes the ranks more reliable and brings the evaluation model broader applicability.

heading: Summary (MCM summary sheet)
evidence: Abstract Our goal is a model that can evaluate the performance of the keep-right-except- to-pass rule and other alternatives by simulating the trafﬁc ﬂow on the freeway.
Our basic lane-changing model focuses on the behavior of a speciﬁc vehicle on the freeway.
We extend our model with a cellular-automaton-based approach.
Four other basic rules such as free-overtaking rule are examined by revising the laws governing the cells in the cellular automaton.
We choose ﬂow rate, average speed as trafﬁc ﬂow criteria, sharp braking fre- quency as a safety criterion and satisfaction and standard deviation of speed as ex- perience criteria.
We change the probability of lane-changing to adjust our model to a country like Great Britain.
Additionally, we reﬁne our extended model considering the ramps.

units.open: Abstract Our goal is a model that can evaluate the performance of the keep-right-except- to-pass rule and other alternatives by simulating the trafﬁc ﬂow on the freeway.
units.close: Then we integrate multi- ple criteria to judge the performance of nine rules using a fuzzy synthetic evalua- tion(FSE).

units.open: Our basic lane-changing model focuses on the behavior of a speciﬁc vehicle on the freeway.
units.close: We carefully examine the vehicle ˛a´rs lane-changing behavior, an essential component of overtaking.

units.open: We extend our model with a cellular-automaton-based approach.
units.close: We can simulate the trafﬁc ﬂow under several conditions by varying the number of lanes, maximum speed limit, minimum speed limit and signaling behavior.

units.open: Four other basic rules such as free-overtaking rule are examined by revising the laws governing the cells in the cellular automaton.
units.close: Then we design ﬁve improved rules based on the basic rules attempting to obtain an optimal rule.

units.open: We choose ﬂow rate, average speed as trafﬁc ﬂow criteria, sharp braking fre- quency as a safety criterion and satisfaction and standard deviation of speed as ex- perience criteria.
units.close: We ﬁnd that in a light trafﬁc case, a partial-assigned-lane-and-keep-right rule performs the best while in a heavy trafﬁc situation, a different-speed-limit-on-each-lane rule is preferred.

units.close: Moreover, we change that parameter to simulate a freeway fully controlled by an intelligent system and observe small deviations.

units.open: Additionally, we reﬁne our extended model considering the ramps.

evidence: To simplify the problem, we make the following basic assumptions, each of which is properly justiﬁed.

• We assume that all drivers act based on the same set of rules.

Based on the basic rules, we propose four improved rules by modifying or com- bining the ﬁve basic rules.
• The partial-assigned-lane rule: cars are assigned to the middle lane and the leftmost lane with the permission to change between these two lanes.

• The minimum-speed-on-leftmost-lane rule: It sets a special minimum speed for the leftmost lane.
• The partial-assigned-lane-and-keep-right rule: We combine the partial- assigned-lane rule and the keep-right-except-to-pass rule to make this rule.

units.open: Based on the basic rules, we propose four improved rules by modifying or com- bining the ﬁve basic rules.
units.close: When creating the rules, we consider not only the implementation of the rules but the overall quality of trafﬁc ﬂow, safety and experience as well.

units.open: • The partial-assigned-lane rule: cars are assigned to the middle lane and the leftmost lane with the permission to change between these two lanes.
units.close: We present this rule because cars account for 60% of the total vehicles and they have relatively high speed.

units.open: • The truck-on-rightmost-lane-only rule: It requires trucks to stick to the rightmost lane while cars and buses can change between the three lanes.
units.close: We present this rule because trucks have the lowest speed and they may constrain the speed of others if they appear on the passing lane.

units.open: • The minimum-speed-on-leftmost-lane rule: It sets a special minimum speed for the leftmost lane.
units.close: We hope it will help increase the efﬁciency of the leftmost passing lane.

units.open: • The partial-assigned-lane-and-keep-right rule: We combine the partial- assigned-lane rule and the keep-right-except-to-pass rule to make this rule.
units.close: We hope this rule can have the merits of previous two rules.

heading: Restatement of the Problem, Literature Review and Our Approach
evidence: The problem needs us to build a mathematical model to finding out the best all time college coach.

There are many Evaluation methods of Coaching all over the world, which include Peer Review, Questionnaire Survey, Bibliometrics method, Analytic Hierarchy Process and Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation Method etc.
 Questionnaire Survey: A research instrument consisting of a series of questions and other prompts for the purpose of gathering information from respondents.

We analyzed the problems above and consulted lots of literature, and then come up with the following approaches.

In this paper, we integrated with the AHP and FCE, obtained the fuzzy comprehensive evaluation model based on analytic hierarchy process (AHP-FCE).

heading: 1 Problem Statement and 2 Planned Approach
evidence: Top Coaches of the Last 100 Years .
Because coaches inﬂuence both the per- formance and reputation of the teams they lead, a question of great concern to universities, players, and fans alike is: Who is the best coach in a given sport?
Our objective is to rank the top 5 coaches in each of 3 diﬀerent college-level sports.

heading: 3 Assumptions
evidence: Due to limited data about the coaching habits of all coaches at all teams over the last century in various collegiate sports, we use the following assumptions to 3 Team #30680 Page 4 of 18 complete our model.
• The skill level of a coach is ultimately expressed through his/her team’s wins over another and the margin by which they win.
• The skills of teams are constant throughout any given year (ex: No players are injured in the middle of a season).
• Winning k games against a good team improves team skill more than winning k games against an average team.
• The skill of a team is a function of the skill of the players and the skill of the coach.
• The eﬀect of coach skill is only large when the diﬀerence between player skill is small.
• When player skills between two teams are similarly matched, coach skill is the only factor that determines the team that wins and the margin by which they win by.

units.open: Due to limited data about the coaching habits of all coaches at all teams over the last century in various collegiate sports, we use the following assumptions to 3 Team #30680 Page 4 of 18 complete our model.

units.open: • The skill level of a coach is ultimately expressed through his/her team’s wins over another and the margin by which they win.
units.close: Even if the coach signiﬁcantly ampliﬁes the skills of his/her players, he/she still cannot be considered “good” if the team wins no games.

units.open: • The skills of teams are constant throughout any given year (ex: No players are injured in the middle of a season).
units.close: In reality, changing player skills throughout the season make it more diﬃcult to determine the eﬀect of the coach on a game.

units.open: • Winning k games against a good team improves team skill more than winning k games against an average team.
units.close: This assumption is intuitive and allows us to use the eigenvector centrality metric as a measure of total team skill.

units.open: • The skill of a team is a function of the skill of the players and the skill of the coach.
units.close: This assumption is important because it simpliﬁes the relationship between player and coach skill to a point where we can easily optimize coach skill vectors.

units.open: • The eﬀect of coach skill is only large when the diﬀerence between player skill is small.
units.close: However, if two teams are similarly matched in players, a more-skilled coach will make advantageous plays that lead to his/her team winning more often than not.

units.open: • When player skills between two teams are similarly matched, coach skill is the only factor that determines the team that wins and the margin by which they win by.
units.close: By making this assumption, we do not have to account for any other factors.

6.1 When is Coach Skill Important? …
We will now make a key assumption regarding player skill and coach skill.
Think again to a game played between two arbitrary teams A and B.

heading: 8 Testing our Model
evidence: A requirement of any good model is that it must be tolerant to a small amount of error in its inputs.

The ﬁrst intentional source of error that we incorporated into our model was the deletion of a game, speciﬁcally a regular-season win for Alabama (the team with the top-ranked coach in 1975) over Providence with a score of 67 to 60.
The second change that we incorporated was to switch the results of the same game (Alabama 67, Providence 60) to a win for Providence (Providence 67, Alabama 60).
From this analysis we can see that our model follows our predictions accu- rately, and that removing factors that add positively to the skill ranking of a coach is detrimental to their skill value.
The main strength of our approach is that it is able to separate coach proﬁciency from team proﬁciency by calculating probabilities that the historical game data occur given coach skills.
This allows us to more accurately gauge the skills of a coach without factoring in the skills of his/her players.
The main weakness of our model pertains to computational eﬃciency, as our computers could not always adequately calculate all necessary values in our model.
For example, the computer could not ﬁnd the eigenvector centrality values on a small percentage of the graphs, as the Von Mises iteration failed to converge.

heading: Summary sheet
evidence: In recent years, the disappearance of major commercial aircraft over open ocean has led to expensive international search eﬀorts.
• Initial Probability Distribution: We create a prior probability density function to model the potential locations of the missing plane.
• Search Patterns: We implement four independent search patterns and develop a method to measure their eﬀectiveness based on the total probability of ﬁnding the aircraft.
• Dynamic Probability Model: We employ Bayesian Inference to continuously adjust the probabilities of our distribution as information from the search is collected and processed.
• Versatility: We explore variations of crash and search scenarios that realistically simulate actual incidents.

units.open: In recent years, the disappearance of major commercial aircraft over open ocean has led to expensive international search eﬀorts.
units.close: This model assumes that at the moment of lost signal, the plane experiences a failure and is no longer powered.

units.open: • Initial Probability Distribution: We create a prior probability density function to model the potential locations of the missing plane.
units.close: This distribution is based solely on the knowledge that we have about the plane at the time of lost contact: its location, bearing, cruise altitude, and lift-to-drag ratio.

units.open: • Search Patterns: We implement four independent search patterns and develop a method to measure their eﬀectiveness based on the total probability of ﬁnding the aircraft.
units.close: We construct an optimization algorithm to determine the most eﬀective means of conducting each search.

units.open: • Dynamic Probability Model: We employ Bayesian Inference to continuously adjust the probabilities of our distribution as information from the search is collected and processed.
units.close: This allows us to create a posterior probability distribution which reﬁnes the data utilized in subsequent searches.

units.open: • Versatility: We explore variations of crash and search scenarios that realistically simulate actual incidents.
units.close: This adaptability is achieved through the incorporation of adjustable input parameters that reﬂect unique circumstances.

heading: Summary sheet

units.open: In this paper, we develop a model for finding a plane that was lost over a large body of water.
units.close: Our model is very robust and can be used by searchers throughout the entire search process.

units.open: Using only basic information about the flight and its last known location and heading, we are able to carefully calculate the area where the plane might have gone down.

heading: 2.1 Assumptions and Justifications
evidence: Our model makes the following assumptions: …

units.open: Our model makes the following assumptions: …
units.close: Our model makes the following assumptions:

units.open: 1. Generally speaking, the plane crash will occur in the way that will make the search the most diﬃcult.
units.close: This is justiﬁed because assuming the most diﬃcult scenario in modeling makes the model compatible with the most plane crash scenarios.

units.open: 2. We assume that air drag will not a↵ect the distance a plane travels in a crash.
units.close: This is because air drag opposes the forward motion of the plane but also increases the time that the plane remains in forward motion by limiting the speed with which the plane falls.

units.open: 3. Due to the small size of airplane debris, search planes will not be able to use infrared or radar and will have to rely on visual search alone, even in very calm seas.
units.close: Due to the small size of airplane debris, search planes will not be able to use infrared or radar and will have to rely on visual search alone, even in very calm seas.

units.open: 4. The ﬁeld of debris will not scatter so far from the site of the crash that it will change our overall search area.
units.close: Justiﬁcation for this assumption can be found in Section 4.2.

units.open: 5. The area in which the plane crashes is completely water and is ﬂat enough to be modeled as a geometric plane.
units.close: The curvature of the ocean is extremely small and would be insigniﬁcant for all calculations.

units.open: 6. Fatigue of searchers will not impact their e↵ectiveness.
units.close: Fatigue is too diﬃcult to model because it has di↵erent e↵ects on di↵erent individuals, and we can assume further that individuals impaired by fatigue would not be allowed to participate in the search.

units.open: 7. All search planes are assumed to take o↵200 nautical miles from the search location.
units.close: We consider this a reasonable distance, since our model does not know where the nearest land mass or aircraft carrier may be.

units.open: 8. There will be suﬃcient daylight for searching for only 10 hours each day.
units.close: In most locations, this will let searchers start at least one hour after sunrise and end at least one hour before sunset.

units.open: 9. Floating debris will not sink until after the search has been completed.
units.close: Because it’s impossible to accurately model when the debris will sink, we must assume that it has not sunk yet.

heading: 8 Conclusion
evidence: The model we have described in this paper is a robust and comprehensive model that can assist searchers throughout the search for a missing airplane.
In addition, testing our model on di↵erent search methods revealed that there is no one perfect way to search for a missing plane.
There is no one way to search for a missing airplane—there are simply too many unknowns, too many variables, too many things that can go wrong in di↵erent ways.

units.open: The model we have described in this paper is a robust and comprehensive model that can assist searchers throughout the search for a missing airplane.
units.close: Each day, the model can precisely move the search area based on ocean current data, so searchers can know exactly where to focus their e↵orts, and once debris is found, the model can trace the debris back to the original location of the crash.

units.open: In addition, testing our model on di↵erent search methods revealed that there is no one perfect way to search for a missing plane.
units.close: But by testing these algorithms on a variety of scenarios, our model was able to generate recommended search methods for di↵erent search situations.

units.open: There is no one way to search for a missing airplane—there are simply too many unknowns, too many variables, too many things that can go wrong in di↵erent ways.
units.close: But no matter the type of plane, the time it went down, or even the weather, we hope that our model could help searchers at every step of the way.

heading: Summary sheet
evidence: When a plane disappears over remote waters, time is of the essence.
First we investigate how and where airplanes crash and discover that finding a lost plane begins with predicting its location based on variables such as flight speed, glide ratio, and altitude.
● Where to look: ​ Projecting a commercial airplane’s flight path, we construct a Gaussian normal distribution bounded by a rectangular search area.

● Simulate Solutions with Ideal Accuracy: ​ Assuming the search will certainly detect a wreck within radar range,​ ​ we test random flight paths, but they prove inefficient—the most successful takes 38 hours.
● Simulate Solutions with Imperfect Accuracy:​ We now incorporate uncertain detection probability into our model.
● Flexibility: ​ We can easily repurpose our solutions for different numbers of search planes or sizes of crashed planes.
Ultimately, our recommended solution — an application of Bayes' Theorem — takes a realistic and accurate approach to quickly find the majority of lost planes.

heading: 1 Introduction
evidence: Despite modern design and tracking capabilities, airplanes such as Malaysian flight MH370 occasionally disappear over swathes of open ocean.
The primary objective is to find the missing plane.
First we examine historic plane crashes to build context—their locations, causes, and the potential downed planes involved.
We learn about the origin and evolution of ocean search technique.
We research various search planes and sensors to find their speed, sight, and accuracy.
We define all the variables we will use throughout the development of our model.
Using our chosen downed plane specifications, we calculate the maximum search area that we need to consider.
Based on our crash research, we determine the probability distribution of downed planes within the search area.
Using our chosen search plane specifications, we calculate the maximum speed, search sight, and accuracy to be used in our solutions.
We outline all the assumptions we need to begin modeling.
We numerically model lost airplanes with our chosen distribution inside the search area and evaluate random, striped, and sinusoidal search solutions.
Increasing the complexity of our model, we consider what would happen to the search time if we have non-ideal sensor accuracy and redistribute the probability after each pass.
We will simulate our normal model using different inputs to examine the effectiveness and flexibility of our best solutions when searching for varying kinds of downed planes.
Based on our simulation results, we will analyze our generated data and make recommendations for a useful procedure for finding lost airplanes crashed in open water.

heading: 4 Compilation of General Assumptions
evidence: d Search Path: For each variation of the model we will develop one or more solutions that answer the question: how should our search plane determine its route to find the downed plane in the shortest amount of time?
We will assume that the Earth is flat, so planes travel between locations on a linear path.
All airplanes are required to transmit to Air Traffic Control every half an hour.
The airplane will experience the crash -causing failure instantaneously over water somewhere between Point A’ and Point B’, and will not deviate from the flight path until that instant.
This failure is equally likely to occur at any point between A’ and ○ B’.
The airplane will lose all communication capacity during and after the failure.
The airplane cannot travel further than its glide range from the point that failure occurs in any direction from the flight path.
The search area for a Boeing 777 is simplified to a rectangle 520 miles long by 200 miles wide.
The downed airplane will remain on the ocean floor directly under where it lands.
The crash will result in visible debris on the surface of the ocean proportional to the size of the downed airplane.
The probability of containment P(C) follows a normal distribution of three standard deviations across the search area, centered on the flight path.
The debris does not move from directly above the body of the submerged plane.
The search effort will consist of one P-8 Poseidon plane (unless otherwise indicated) that searches continuously at 400 mph until it discovers the debris, without needing to stop for refuel or rest.
Weather or sea conditions will not hinder the search effort or radar visibility.
Cost and fuel are not an issue; the priority is rapidly finding the lost plane.
The search plane will use radar with a sight range of 0 to 10 miles that is uniformly accurate for the entire range.
The time for the search effort to mobilize is negligible and the search plane arrives instantaneously at the search area when calculating total search time.

heading: 8.1 Recommendation
evidence: As we established in the Introduction, the measure of success for our solutions is first, whether they find the lost plane, and second, if they can reasonably expect to rescue plane crash survivors before they die of exposure.

Although all the Striped and Sinusoidal Normal Distribution Solutions’ means are very likely to be below 8 hours, easily fast enough to save the passengers, we do not believe they are realistic enough to recommend.

We recommend the most accurate model and its most successful solution: the Normal Distribution with Discovery Uncertainty (Section 5.2) paired with the Bayesian Search flight path (5.2.1).

heading: 8.2 Strengths and Weaknesses of Recommendation
evidence: Our model takes into account, and can be adjusted for, many different probabilities of detection, search areas, and sight ranges.
The solution locates a high proportion of plane crashes (95% of Boeing-777s and 82% of Cessna-172s) within 24 hours.
The search time is capped at 24 hours due to limitations in computing power because it becomes exponentially harder to use the Bayesian Solution to estimate the best flight path for the next flight.
Although it focuses on areas of high probability, our solution does not entirely eliminate unnecessary overlap especially when transitioning between passes.
Our normal distribution of planes is simplified from the search area design and the standard deviation we estimated has a high degree of uncertainty.
We assume that the search is a one-step process and finding debris means finding the plane, when in reality this could require additional searching.
We discount the time it takes for the search effort to mobilize and for the search plane to arrive at the search area.

heading: 2.4 Assumptions in the Methodology
evidence: There are several assumptions upon which our model and the re- sulting search plan are built.
• The lost plane’s pre-established course is a linear path from point A to point B.
• The lost plane’s glide aﬀects its trajectory into the ocean.
• Any debris disassembles upon impacting the water.
• The plane will not veer more than 3Ghsin(π 8 ) oﬀthe IFP.
• There are no forces (eg. currents) to move the debris or plane from where they ﬁrst landed.
• All planes (lost plane and search plane(s)) in the model are ﬂying at a constant velocity.
• The lost plane is more likely to be found near the last point of communication.
• The lost plane remains aﬂoat (detectable) during the entire time the search is in action.
• Every searching plane has the same instrumentation, searches at the same speed and ﬂies at the same altitude.

heading: 2.6 Strengths and Weaknesses of Our Model, 2.6.1 Strengths and 2.6.2 Weaknesses
evidence: 2.6 Strengths and Weaknesses of Our Model …
2.6.1 Strengths …
Our outlined model has particular strengths, unavailable in other Search and Rescue methods.
Here, we carefully construct a decreasing, concave down distribution to account for the large likelihood that complications arise early after y0.
When k = 1, the search occurs in perfect conditions, while k = 0.5 may indicate some fog, choppy water, or other inhibiting factors.
Our search plan is a constantly updating algorithm keeping time eﬃciency in mind.
It is important to consider the weaknesses of our model that may be worth addressing in the future.
The standard deviation was calculated using trigonometry, indicating that our rectangular probability region is based on a triangular calculation.
Another weakness to consider is the lack of consideration of cur- rents in each of our partitioned search regions.

units.open: Our outlined model has particular strengths, unavailable in other Search and Rescue methods.
units.close: In many Search and Rescue Methodologies, it is assumed that the time of casualty is uniformly distributed over all possible times in a given range (Lawrence 1977).

units.open: Here, we carefully construct a decreasing, concave down distribution to account for the large likelihood that complications arise early after y0.
units.close: The POD incorporates several factors, including an added constant k.

units.open: When k = 1, the search occurs in perfect conditions, while k = 0.5 may indicate some fog, choppy water, or other inhibiting factors.
units.close: This constant helps to better explain the rate of coverage while still using Koopman’s commonly-used Exponential Model.

units.open: Our search plan is a constantly updating algorithm keeping time eﬃciency in mind.

heading: 2 Introduction
evidence: Approaching its anniversary, the missing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370) on March 8, 2014 has become one of the mysteries in aviation his- tory.
With deepest condolences to the victims, authorities are pondering how to establish a more efﬁcient and accurate maritime search and rescue (SAR) simu- lation system.
Our goal is to construct a generic and reliable mathematic model correspond- ing to a lost plane, which is feared to have crashed in open water in the way to point B from point A.
• Establish a collision model to determine the number of drifters resulting from the crash.
• Propose a search model based on Bayes’ theorem, considering water sur- face search and underwater search sequentially to optimize on search ar- eas.
• Develop an allocation model to match search planes with search areas.
• Employ the preceding approach in the case of ﬁnding AF447 at the fourth attempt to verify the credibility of our model.
• Predict the possible location of MH370 wreckage with accessible data and offer advice to assist the further search effort.
• Analyze the strengths and weaknesses inherent in the model and conﬁrm the potential development direction.

heading: Summary sheet
evidence: - ‘Kowalski, visual of debris at 9’o clock;’ - ‘Half of North America just lost their Facebook.’ Well, the lines above from the movie Gravity might be slightly exaggerate, but it would more or less be real if we do nothing about the threatening space debris.

In this paper, we focus on evaluating potential commercial opportunities in removing space debris that is currently revolving around the Earth in low Earth orbit since the growing number of aerospace debris has been a major concern around the world community.
The first of the three models proposed presents a time-dependent evaluation method that projects potential economic profits for 15 consecutive years.
The second of the three models helps to better assess the compensation level by estimating the probability of a collision between the existing debris and lately launched satellites.
The third of the three models jumps out of the two parties previously discussed and shifts to a third body, the policy maker.
Admittedly, the potential profits projected in the first model appear to be quite sensitive to the insurance commission determinant.

Based on the data and figures returned from the models above, we conclude with confidence that the commercial opportunities do exist if the private firm chooses the land-based and space-based combined alternative.

heading: Executive Summary
evidence: We shall first imagine the following scenario, ‘Half of North America just lost their Facebook.’ The famous line from Gravity may not be exaggerate.
Considering the significance and urgency of this issue, a chorus of furious space specialists pilloried the inaction of some politicians and developed multiple ways to eliminate space debris.
We raised three models from distinguishing perspective.
We classified the prevailing methods of removing space debris into two categories, namely, the land-based alternative and the space-based alternative.
The land-based alternative requires a huge amount of initial investment and, thus, needs a relatively long period of time to gain a net profit.
On the other side, the space-based alternative requires relatively less initial investment.

Due to the obvious advantages and weaknesses of each alternative, it makes sense to run this model for a third time with these two alternatives combined, which means we deploy land- based alternative and space-based alternative simultaneously.
A game theory analysis is also carried out in the third model.
Further conducted sensitivity analysis also reveals several interesting points.
The application of recyclable rockets that could be used in space-based alternative does not make a huge difference to the firm’s net profit.
The sensitivity test of the insurance commission parameter shows that this variable can be essential for the firm to make a profit in the early stage of simulations.
Therefore, we shall formally conclude that the combined alternative is an optimal method to tackle the space debris issue for the private firm.

units.open: Further conducted sensitivity analysis also reveals several interesting points.
units.close: A pattern of diminishing return for each 1% decrease is also shown from data gathered.

units.open: The application of recyclable rockets that could be used in space-based alternative does not make a huge difference to the firm’s net profit.
units.close: Further, total profits increased by only 0.38 billion for each additional lifetime increase.

units.open: Therefore, we shall formally conclude that the combined alternative is an optimal method to tackle the space debris issue for the private firm.

heading: 1.2 Our Work
evidence: We are asked to find out whether an economically attractive opportunity exist and develop a model to determine the best alternative or combination of alternatives that a private firm could adopt as a commercial opportunity to address the space debris problem.

Since the rising population of space debris has strongly affected the safety of the spacecraft and most of insurers didn’t take this situation into consideration, a good commercial opportunity arose: debris collision space insurance.
We firstly build a general insurance model.
We simulate the whole insurance service via computer.

heading: Problem Solution, Business Model and Action Recommendation
evidence: “The greatest risk to space missions comes from non-trackable debris,” said Nicholas Johnson, NASA chief scientist for orbital debris.
Active Debris Removal (ADR) is a very effective solution to reduce the collision occurrence possibility.
However, even though ADR is effective to lower the risk induced by space debris, ADR cost exceeds the benefit brought by ADR, it is hard to carry out ADR.
Most of the owners of the satellites tend to cover insurance for their spacecraft in the past decade.
We offer the owners of satellites a special space insurance serve which consists of two parts.
How to choose the suitable ADR methods among all developed ADR methods is a critical problem, both to our business model and all the space faring parties.
We build up a model to determine which ADR methods to be used, considering the manufacture costs, cost of using, applicability to remove the debris in certain size and time consuming of the methods.
Based on our model, we can come to a conclusion that laser has the best applicability in most situation.
For the governments, improving space environment is extremely relevant to the space development.
· Raise the awareness of space debris problem.
· Provide policy support and fund subsidy for the private company related to space debris, such as our company.

units.close: In order to conquer this situation, we create a new business model, which can both provide commercial benefits and reduce the space debris.

heading: Summary
evidence: With the rapid increment of the trafﬁc ﬂow, the problem of merging after the toll barriers has risen public concern.

First, we classify the area following the toll barrier which may already be imple- mented into eight kinds according to the different shapes, sizes, and merging patterns of the area based on the toll plazas in reality.
Second, we use VISSIM to do the simulation of the typical eight models of the area following the toll barrier.
Third, we build a comprehensive evaluation model based on PCA to evaluate the eight typical models and the optimum model we build.
Fourth, in order to obtain a better solution, we build two models to obtain the opti- mum solution.

heading: Letter to the New Jersey Turnpike Authority
evidence: Dear New Jersey Turnpike Authority, …
We are here to help you with determining if there are better solutions of the merging area following the toll barrier than any in common use.
As we all known, the main purpose of researching the problem of merge after toll is to control the cost and to improve the throughput and the safety of the area as much as possible at the same time.
Firstly, before proposing a better solution, we should research the advantages and the disadvantages of the existing models.
Secondly, we build a simulation model to obtain the important parameters of the corresponding model, such as trafﬁc ﬂow, average queuing time, average time of delay, etc.
Thirdly, we build a comprehensive evaluation model based on PCA to evaluate the eight models listed above.
On the basis of existing models, we propose a better solution.
In reality, when the vehicles entering the area following the toll barrier, they always want to get into the travel lanes as soon as possible.
In accordance with the above research ideas, we develop a better design of the area following the toll barrier.
Of course, a good design can not only work efﬁciently under normal circumstances, but also can keep running under some speciﬁc extreme circumstances.
The ﬁrst one is to change the value of trafﬁc ﬂow: at the small trafﬁc ﬂow, our model can run smoothly, but the number of tollbooths may exceeds the demand.
The second aspect is the situation when more autonomous(self-driving) vehicles are added to the trafﬁc ﬂow.

Considering the proportions of different kinds of tollbooths which indicated by the service time, our model can be modiﬁed by adjusting the merging pattern to accommo- date to the speciﬁc situation in which we cite two speciﬁc examples in our paper.

units.close: This letter explains our optimum solution model, and provide a series of suggestions under various circumstances.

units.open: As we all known, the main purpose of researching the problem of merge after toll is to control the cost and to improve the throughput and the safety of the area as much as possible at the same time.
units.close: Thus our model is built based on these three factors.

units.open: Firstly, before proposing a better solution, we should research the advantages and the disadvantages of the existing models.
units.close: We collect the characteristics of the existing models according to the shape of the area, the size of the area and the merging pattern of the area and classify them into eight kinds.

units.open: Secondly, we build a simulation model to obtain the important parameters of the corresponding model, such as trafﬁc ﬂow, average queuing time, average time of delay, etc.
units.close: econdly, we build a simulation model to obtain the important parameters of the corresponding model, such as trafﬁc ﬂow, average queuing time, average time of delay, etc.

units.open: Thirdly, we build a comprehensive evaluation model based on PCA to evaluate the eight models listed above.
units.close: In this way, we get the best model which is in the shape of isosceles trapezoid with stipulated merging pattern and medium size of the area among the eight existing models.

units.open: On the basis of existing models, we propose a better solution.
units.close: We can get the optimum number of tollbooths and the optimum height of the trapezoid area while minimizing the total cost of the area.

units.open: In reality, when the vehicles entering the area following the toll barrier, they always want to get into the travel lanes as soon as possible.
units.close: In this way, we reduce the number of merging points of the area, increase the throughput of the area and promote the accident prevention of the area.

units.open: In accordance with the above research ideas, we develop a better design of the area following the toll barrier.
units.close: n accordance with the above research ideas, we develop a better design of the area following the toll barrier.

units.open: Of course, a good design can not only work efﬁciently under normal circumstances, but also can keep running under some speciﬁc extreme circumstances.
units.close: To this end, we perform several analysis to test our model.

units.open: The ﬁrst one is to change the value of trafﬁc ﬂow: at the small trafﬁc ﬂow, our model can run smoothly, but the number of tollbooths may exceeds the demand.
units.close: We can adjust our merging pattern to divert the trafﬁc.

units.open: The second aspect is the situation when more autonomous(self-driving) vehicles are added to the trafﬁc ﬂow.
units.close: Due to the safety and the efﬁciency of autonomous vehicles, we do not have to stipulate the merge pattern of the area following the toll barrier which can bring the advantages of autonomous vehicles to the full play.

units.open: Considering the proportions of different kinds of tollbooths which indicated by the service time, our model can be modiﬁed by adjusting the merging pattern to accommo- date to the speciﬁc situation in which we cite two speciﬁc examples in our paper.

units.open: The purpose of this letter is to advise you on the design of the toll plaza.
units.close: Here we will introduce the design of the toll plaza from three aspects.

units.open: The first is to determine the number of toll lanes.

heading: 8 Conclusions
evidence: Toll roads, and their associated toll plazas are an unpleasant, but in many cases unavoidable, part of life.
Our model suggests that the shape of the merge lanes that bottleneck traﬃc after the toll plazas have the most signiﬁcant impact on overall satisfaction within a system.
When designing toll plazas, particular attention should be paid to preserving driver patience.

units.open: Toll roads, and their associated toll plazas are an unpleasant, but in many cases unavoidable, part of life.
units.close: Overall, our model allowed us to look at the impact of individual choice upon the dynamics of queueing at a toll plaza.

units.open: Our model suggests that the shape of the merge lanes that bottleneck traﬃc after the toll plazas have the most signiﬁcant impact on overall satisfaction within a system.
units.close: In particular, a symmetrical lane merge is more eﬃcient than a skewed merge from one direction.

units.open: When designing toll plazas, particular attention should be paid to preserving driver patience.
units.close: Perhaps a simple solution, like decreasing the speed limit half a mile before the toll plaza, so that drivers simply drive slow as opposed to stopping, could drastically improve the eﬃciency of the entire system.

heading: Summary
evidence: With the advent of increasingly accelerated globalization, the intricate ge- ographic distributions of languages start to hamper international business op- erations and cross-culture interactions.
Our model focuses on native speakers and non-native speakers of lan- guages.
It has been tested that our matrix only requires relatively little amount of data input to function well.

units.open: With the advent of increasingly accelerated globalization, the intricate ge- ographic distributions of languages start to hamper international business op- erations and cross-culture interactions.
units.close: Therefore, we establish a new model to replace the projection model based purely on population, as it is not only inaccurate but also invalid faced with the scarcity of supporting data.

heading: 3. Transportation Capability Evaluation Model, 3.2 to 3.4 and 5.1 Schedule Arrangement Model
evidence: In this section, we will evaluate transportation ability of each type of drones.
• All Cargo Containers(CC), Drone (in shipping containers), Drone Cargo Bays (DCB), and Medical packages (MP) are cuboids.
• Drones and Drone Cargo Bays should be placed into Cargo Containers in parallel, which is "parallel placement".
• The thickness of Drone Cargo Bays can be neglected.

heading: Memo to CEO of HELP, Inc.
evidence: Memo to CEO of HELP, Inc.

In the post-disaster relief, unmanned aerial vehicles, also called drones, are not limited by road conditions, so they can quickly provide medicines and other urgent materials to the af- fected areas, which can alleviate the shortage of local post-disaster med …
In 2017, the worst hurricane to ever hit the United States territory of Puerto Rico left the island with severe damage.
We designed a prototype of the DroneGo system based on ofﬁcial drone, medicine and con- tainer information and applied it to the disaster situation in Puerto Rico.

Firstly, for the loading problem of drone ﬂeet, we use an indicator of drone ﬂeet transport capacity to form our drone Transport Capacity Model to solve the problem of maximizing the drone ﬂeet medicine transport capacity when the disaster location is unknown.

Secondly, if we got the information of the disaster area, we can use our DroneGo system based on spatial geographic information, which integrated the previous drone Transportation Capability Model and a drone Reconnaissance Capability Model.
We use an integer programming model and an improved greedy algorithm to construct the Schedule Arrangement Model and Route Arrangement Model of drones.
If you want to know more details, please read our essay about this subject.

heading: Go Safe with Drones — Summary
evidence: Go Safe with Drones Summary We use Dijkstra Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to develop a set of models which can solve for a universally practicable DroneGo disaster response system.
Before model construction, we make some basic assumptions essential to further analyses.
First, we rebuild a three-dimensional map by interpolation with intensive data col- lection.
Next, we design an optimization model for delivery to minimize the total deliv- ering time.
Based on two models above, we build a combined model to address multi-objective optimization problems.
In addition, we apply our models to Haiti’s earthquake in 2010 to test the prac- ticability and effectiveness.
Finally, we conduct sensitivity analyses and prove our models to be quite robust against the changes in the method of assigning settlement’s importance.

heading: Multi-Directional Comprehensive Disaster Response System Based on Optimization — Summary
evidence: According to the actual situation of Puerto Rico, we designed a disaster response system from the perspective of disaster area demand, company cost, realizability and security.
First, we identified the number and type of UAVs(unmanned aerial vehicle) in the UAV fleet based on the geographical location and needs of Puerto Rican hospitals.
Second, we designed the packaging configuration for containers.
Third, we gridded the main roads in Puerto Rico's main disaster areas and transformed the continuous problems into discrete ones.
Fourth, the payload packaging configuration of UAV is designed by using optimization methods.
Fifth, in order to make the UAV reconnaissance the road as wide as possible, flight schedule of the UAV are obtained by using ant colony optimization (ACO).
To sum up, we considered many factors to design DroneGo system.

heading: A Simulation Based Assessment of Sandcastle Foundation — Summary
evidence: Sandcastle building is a common way to recreating for beach goers.
In order to explore the most stable three-dimensional geometric shape, we establish a periodic sand-water cell automaton model to experiment with the most likely mul- tiple geometric shapes.

In the model, we formulate the state transition rules through multivariate analy- sis based on multi-criteria judgments, and carry out quantitative calculations on the waves’ sediment carrying and capillary phenomena between sand and water.
In the practice of building sand castles, it was found that different sand-to-water mixture ratios also played a crucial role in the sand foundations’ stability.
In order to study rain’s effect on the result, we introduce a rainfall module based on the original model.
Sensitivity analysis shows the strong robustness of our model.
In addition, our model is easy to implement and extend.

units.open: Sandcastle building is a common way to recreating for beach goers.
units.close: Therefore, how to establish a stable foundation is of great signiﬁcance to the duration of sand castles.

units.open: In order to explore the most stable three-dimensional geometric shape, we establish a periodic sand-water cell automaton model to experiment with the most likely mul- tiple geometric shapes.
units.close: The optimum geometric shape we obtain is triangle frustum.

units.open: In order to study rain’s effect on the result, we introduce a rainfall module based on the original model.
units.close: We ﬁnd that the original best geometry does not the only one which perform well under rainfall conditions, and ellipse frustum is the another better geometry when it is rainy.

units.open: Sensitivity analysis shows the strong robustness of our model.

heading: How to build a durable sandcastle foundation? — Summary
evidence: In recent years, as sand castle art has become more popular, more and more ingenious sand castle art works have been created.
First, the optimal geometry considering the dual erosion effects of waves and tides is determined.
Secondly, the optimal water-sand mixing ratio is determined.
Further, an optimal geometry considering rain erosion is determined.
Finally, we use the method of humidifying and spraying the adhesive when the air humidity is the lowest to improve the stability of the sand castle foundation.

units.open: In recent years, as sand castle art has become more popular, more and more ingenious sand castle art works have been created.
units.close: However, perfect works of art will disappear, and how to be preserved for a long time becomes an obstacle to the advancement of Sandcastle art.

units.open: First, the optimal geometry considering the dual erosion effects of waves and tides is determined.
units.close: Finally, we use a Discrete Global Optimization Algorithm Based on Successive Descent Methods to determine the shape of the optimal sandcastle foundation as a cylinder.

units.open: Secondly, the optimal water-sand mixing ratio is determined.
units.close: We again use the discrete global optimization algorithm based on the successive descent method to efficiently find the optimal water-sand mix ratio of 0.739.

units.open: Further, an optimal geometry considering rain erosion is determined.
units.close: Considering two indicators of anti-erosion ability and establishing a fuzzy comprehensive evaluation model, we determine that the optimal shape is still a cylinder.

units.open: Finally, we use the method of humidifying and spraying the adhesive when the air humidity is the lowest to improve the stability of the sand castle foundation.
units.close: Finally, we decided to humidify the sandcastle foundation and spray the adhesive at 13:30 on a cloudy day and 13:00 on a sunny day.

heading: Article for Fun in the Sun — How to build a perfect sandcastle?
evidence: Article for Fun in the Sun How to build a perfect sandcastle?
Have you ever tried to build a sandcastle when you are at the beach?
Some people may think that building sandcastle is just a mechanical building game like building a house, other people may consider it as a game identifying combinations of different shapes.
First, we need to understand why a sandcastle could stand before explaining the best method to build a perfect sandcastle.
Now you have known the reason behind the sandcastle's standing.

In order to find the most suitable shape for building the sandcastle foundation, taking the factors that threaten the sandcastle into account, such as frequent and rapid waves and gradually rising tides, we built the sandcastle-erosion model.

By simulating the residual states of sandcastles of different shapes under different erosion conditions under the same volume and comparing them, we finally get the best geometry for sandcastle foundation.
Since the ratio of sand to water is important to the success of a sandcastle, the golden ratio of sand to water is also a concern for sandcastle builders.
People usually choose to play by the beach on a sunny day.
How's that? After looking at the results of our models, I believe you can also build a perfect sandcastle.

heading: Summary Sheet — The Longest Lasting Sandcastle
evidence: A variety of sandcastles can be found on the seashore, range from simple mounds of sand to complex castle replicas.
In task 1, in order to identity the best 3D geometric shape of sandcastle foundation, firstly, our team choose six common geometric shapes to analyze.
In task 2, take sand-to-water mixture proportion into consideration.

heading: Summary Sheet — ‘Rapid Bushfire Response’ UAV System
evidence: Due to the drought of southeast Australia, forest fires burn across the country, impacting New South Wales and eastern Victoria.

For model 1, to address the irregularity of fire regions and SSA drones’ information acquisition areas, we used regional discretization method, turning fire data and multi-drone cooperation in to con- straint equations.

heading: Summary Sheet — Rapid Bushfire Response for Emergency Response
evidence: How to respond and deal with ﬁres in time when they occur is a question worth thinking about.
In Task 1, the paper establishes the area safety evaluation model with ﬁre frequency, size, and recent ﬁre situation as indicators to classify the danger levels of different areas in Victoria.

units.open: To simplify the problem, we make the following basic assumptions, each of which is properly justified.
units.close: Other assumptions may not be as follows, but will be put forward in the model later.

units.open: Assumption 1: The occurrence of a fire is predictable.
units.close: ⚫  Justification: Although the occurrence of forest fires is random, we assume the possible fire location can be predicted by the weather conditions and locations of frequent outbreaks in the past.

units.open: Assumption 2: More than one EOC is located in the southeast corner of Australia.
units.close: So we assume that multiple EOCs can be built to meet the support requirements.

units.open: Assumption 3: Fire caused by malicious destruction is not considered during the wildfires in ⚫ the scope of research.
units.close: Therefore, unpredictable malicious fire causes can be ignored.

units.open: Assumption 4: All drones & equipment and EOC are reliable for fire rescue without con- ⚫ sidering biological death and injury.
units.close: Therefore, we believe that our drones & equipment and EOC are completely reliable in our model and the loss of life is not as a measure of the effectiveness in our response.

units.open: Assumption 5: Assume the research data is accurate.
units.close: ⚫  Justification: We assume that economic costs for EOCs and drones do not show obvious measurable deviation, so we can establish a more reasonable model based on it.

heading: Decision System for Optimizing Water Allocation
evidence: Construction of dams in the Colorado Basin provides people with abundant water re- sources.
For Question 1, firstly, we analyze the principle of hydropower conversion , the cou- pling characteristics of cascade hydropower stations and the line loss of electricity trans- mission.
For Question 2, we construct a competitive game model of water resource allocation according to competing interest between general usage and electricity production, as well as between five states.
For Question 3, we first introduce water-shortage index SI to characterize degree of the negative impact of water shortage in each states.
For Question 4, firstly, the water allocation strategy is analyzed when the demands of each state fluctuate over time.
Keywords: Simulated Annealing, Game Theory,Newton Iteration, Water-Shortage Index Contents 1 Introduction 4 1.1 Problem background .

units.open: Construction of dams in the Colorado Basin provides people with abundant water re- sources.
units.close: However, with the change of climate and people’s over-exploitation of water resources, the water levels of dams continue to decrease, threatening economic develop- ment and ecological environment in the surrounding areas.

units.open: For Question 1, firstly, we analyze the principle of hydropower conversion , the cou- pling characteristics of cascade hydropower stations and the line loss of electricity trans- mission.
units.close: The optimal water addition time interval is 2 days and additional water volume is 5.22 × 108m3/day .

units.open: For Question 2, we construct a competitive game model of water resource allocation according to competing interest between general usage and electricity production, as well as between five states.
units.close: … ifferential equations of the net profits of each state are obtained, and the Newton iteration method is used to solve the Nash equilibrium point of the game, so as to obtain the water supply and power supply strategy that maximizes the interests of each state.

units.open: For Question 3, we first introduce water-shortage index SI to characterize degree of the negative impact of water shortage in each states.
units.close: The results of the model show that when there is a serious shortage of water resources, people tend to use limited water resources to meet the demands of general usage.

units.open: For Question 4, firstly, the water allocation strategy is analyzed when the demands of each state fluctuate over time.
units.close: It is found that the hydropower allocated to each state is significantly decreased, and there is a significant low water supply in dry season.
